title: Islamic Golden Age music's secret organ that reshaped medieval sound

beats.say: But the real surprise: the Andalusian city of Córdoba hosted a hidden choir of Persian musicians fleeing the Abbasid decline.
In 958, the Caliph al-Hakam ordered them to transcribe Greek lyre scales onto parchment, birthing the maqam system.
Their secret: a water-powered organ called the naqqāra, built by engineer al-Mawardi, could sustain a drone for hours.
When the Seljuks conquered Baghdad in 1055, they seized the instrument, spreading its resonance across Persia's deserts.
By 1120, the famed poet-musician Ibn Bābū taught the naqqāra to Sufi mystics, who used its hum for trance rituals.
Their melodies traveled west, inspiring the Christian troubadour's lute in Valencia, a cross-cultural echo unheard by historians.
Yet the instrument vanished after the Mongol sack of 1258, its blueprints burned, leaving only cryptic verses.
Centuries later, archaeologists uncovered a naqqāra fragment in Samarkand, confirming the myth was fact.
So the Islamic Golden Age's hidden soundtrack reshaped medieval music, a secret legacy waiting to be heard.
